claims.source: Indeed, removing stxbp1b, one of the two STXBP1 homologs in zebrafish, caused spontaneous electrographic seizures (Grone et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction with a citation supporting it.

claims.claim: Three different Stxbp1 null alleles have been generated in mice.
claims.source: Three different Stxbp1 null alleles have been generated in mice (Verhage, 2000; Miyamoto et al., 2017; Kovacevic et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction with citations supporting it.

claims.claim: Stxbp1 protein levels were reduced by only 25% in the brain of one line of previous Stxbp1 heterozygous knockout mice.
claims.source: Interestingly, Stxbp1 protein levels were reduced by only 25% in the brain of one line of previous Stxbp1 heterozygous knockout mice (Orock et al., 2018) and 25% in the cortex and 50% in the hippocampus of another line (Miyamoto et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction with citations supporting it.

claims.claim: Stxbp1 protein levels were reduced by 25% in the cortex and 50% in the hippocampus of another line of Stxbp1 heterozygous knockout mice.
claims.source: Interestingly, Stxbp1 protein levels were reduced by only 25% in the brain of one line of previous Stxbp1 heterozygous knockout mice (Orock et al., 2018) and 25% in the cortex and 50% in the hippocampus of another line (Miyamoto et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction with citations supporting it.

claims.claim: Homozygous mutants (Stxbp1tm1d/tm1d and Stxbp1tm1a/tm1a) died immediately after birth because they were completely paralyzed and could not breathe.
claims.source: Homozygous mutants (Stxbp1tm1d/tm1d and Stxbp1tm1a/tm1a) died immediately after birth because they were completely paralyzed and could not breathe, consistent with the previous Stxbp1 null alleles (Verhage, 2000; Miyamoto et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and is supported by observation of the mice and citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: At embryonic day 17.5, Stxbp1 protein was absent in Stxbp1tm1d/tm1d and Stxbp1tm1a/tm1a mice, and reduced by 50% in Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice.
claims.source: Western blots with antibodies recognizing either the N- or C-terminus of Stxbp1 showed that at embryonic day 17.5, Stxbp1 protein was absent in Stxbp1tm1d/tm1d and Stxbp1tm1a/tm1a mice, and reduced by 50% in Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C), indicating that both tm1d and tm1a are null alleles.
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C.

claims.claim: Both tm1d and tm1a are null alleles.
claims.source: Western blots with antibodies recognizing either the N- or C-terminus of Stxbp1 showed that at embryonic day 17.5, Stxbp1 protein was absent in Stxbp1tm1d/tm1d and Stxbp1tm1a/tm1a mice, and reduced by 50% in Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C), indicating that both tm1d and tm1a are null alleles.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on Western blot data showing absence of protein in homozygous mutants.

claims.claim: Stxbp1 was reduced by 40–50% in most brain areas of Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice at 3 months of age except the cerebellum and olfactory bulb where the reduction was 20–30%.
claims.source: We surveyed the Stxbp1 protein levels in different brain regions of Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice at 3 months of age. Stxbp1 was reduced by 40–50% in most brain areas except the cerebellum and olfactory bulb where the reduction was 20–30% (Figure 1B,C).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1B,C.

claims.claim: Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ are Stxbp1 haploinsufficient mice.
claims.source: These results demonstrate that Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ are indeed Stxbp1 haploinsufficient mice.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the Western blot data showing reduced protein levels.

claims.claim: At the time of genotyping (around postnatal week 3), Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice are 40% and 43% of the total offspring, respectively, indicating a postnatal lethality phenotype.
claims.source: We bred Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice with WT mice and found that at the time of genotyping (i.e., around postnatal week 3) Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice are 40% and 43% of the total offspring, respectively (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), indicating a postnatal lethality phenotype.
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by genotyping data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: Stxbp1 haploinsufficient mice show reduced survival, but this phenotype is not fully penetrant.
claims.source: Thus, Stxbp1 haploinsufficient mice show reduced survival, but this phenotype is not fully penetrant.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the survival data.

claims.claim: The body weights of Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice were consistently about 20% less than their sex- and age-matched WT littermates.
claims.source: Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice appeared smaller and their body weights were consistently about 20% less than their sex- and age-matched WT littermates (Figure 1E,F).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by body weight data shown in Figure 1F.

claims.claim: At 4 weeks of age, Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice began to exhibit abnormal hindlimb clasping, indicative of dystonia or spasticity.
claims.source: At 4 weeks of age, Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice began to exhibit abnormal hindlimb clasping, indicative of dystonia or spasticity (Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 1E and 1G.

claims.claim: By the age of 3 months, almost all Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice developed hindlimb clasping.
claims.source: By the age of 3 months, almost all mutant mice developed hindlimb clasping (Figure 1G).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 1G.

claims.claim: Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice traveled longer distances and faster than WT mice in the open-field test, indicating that Stxbp1 haploinsufficient mice are hyperactive.
claims.source: The locomotion of Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice was largely normal, but they traveled longer distances and faster than WT mice, indicating that Stxbp1 haploinsufficient mice are hyperactive (Figure 2B,C).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by open-field test data shown in Figure 2B,C.

claims.claim: Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice explored the center region of the arena less than WT mice and made less vertical movements, indicating that the mutant mice are more anxious.
claims.source: Both Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice explored the center region of the arena less than WT mice (Figure 2D) and made less vertical movements (Figure 2E), indicating that the mutant mice are more anxious.
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by open-field test data shown in Figure 2D,E.

claims.claim: The forelimb grip strength of Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice was weaker than WT mice.
claims.source: However, the forelimb grip strength of Stxbp1 haploinsufficient mice was weaker (Figure 2F).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by grip strength test data shown in Figure 2F.

claims.claim: In the foot slip test, both Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice made many more foot slips than WT mice.
claims.source: Furthermore, in the foot slip test where a mouse is allowed to walk on a wire grid, both Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice were not able to place their paws precisely on the wire to hold themselves and made many more foot slips than WT mice (Figure 2G).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by foot slip test data shown in Figure 2G.

claims.claim: In the vertical pole test, it took Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice longer to orient themselves downward and descend the pole than WT mice.
claims.source: To assess the agility of mice, we performed the vertical pole test, which is often used to measure the bradykinesia of parkinsonism. When mice were placed head-up on the top of a vertical pole, it took mutant mice longer to orient themselves downward and descend the pole than WT mice (Figure 2H).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by vertical pole test data shown in Figure 2H.

claims.claim: Stxbp1 haploinsufficient mice do not develop ataxia, but their fine motor coordination and muscle strength are reduced.
claims.source: Together, these results indicate that Stxbp1 haploinsufficient mice do not develop ataxia, but their fine motor coordination and muscle strength are reduced.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the motor function tests.

claims.claim: Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice showed normal startle responses to different levels of sound.
claims.source: We next examined the acoustic sensory function and found that Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice showed normal startle responses to different levels of sound (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by acoustic startle test data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice displayed similar pre-pulse inhibition as WT mice.
claims.source: To test sensorimotor gating, we measured the pre-pulse inhibition where the startle response to a strong sound is reduced by a preceding weaker sound. Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice displayed similar pre-pulse inhibition as WT mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by pre-pulse inhibition test data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claims.claim: Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice had normal nociception as measured by the hot plate test.
claims.source: They also had normal nociception as measured by the hot plate test (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by hot plate test data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claims.claim: The sensory functions and sensorimotor gating of Stxbp1 haploinsufficient mice are normal.
claims.source: Thus, the sensory functions and sensorimotor gating of Stxbp1 haploinsufficient mice are normal.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the sensory function tests.

claims.claim: When tested with an inter-trial interval of 24 hr in the novel object recognition test, WT mice interacted more with the novel object than the familiar object, whereas Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice interacted equally between the familiar and novel objects.
claims.source: When tested with an inter-trial interval of 24 hr, WT mice interacted more with the novel object than the familiar object, whereas Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice interacted equally between the familiar and novel objects (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by novel object recognition test data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Both long-term and short-term recognition memories are impaired in Stxbp1 haploinsufficient mice.
claims.source: Thus, both long-term and short-term recognition memories are impaired in Stxbp1 haploinsufficient mice.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the novel object recognition test data with different inter-trial intervals.

claims.claim: At two tested ages, Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice displayed a profound reduction in both context- and cue-induced freezing behaviors when tested 24 hr after the fear conditioning paradigm.
claims.source: At two tested ages, Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice displayed a profound reduction in both context- and cue-induced freezing behaviors when tested 24 hr after the conditioning paradigm (Figure 3B–E).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by fear conditioning test data shown in Figure 3B–E.

claims.claim: Stxbp1 haploinsufficiency impairs both hippocampus-dependent contextual and hippocampus-independent cued fear memories.
claims.source: Since the acoustic startle response and nociception are intact in Stxbp1 haploinsufficient mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,C), these results indicate that Stxbp1 haploinsufficiency impairs both hippocampus-dependent contextual and hippocampus-independent cued fear memories.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the fear conditioning test data and the normal sensory functions.

claims.claim: Both long-term and short-term forms of recognition and associative memories are severely impaired in Stxbp1 haploinsufficiency mice, but their working memory is intact.
claims.source: Taken together, our results indicate that both long-term and short-term forms of recognition and associative memories are severely impaired in Stxbp1 haploinsufficiency mice, but their working memory is intact.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the cognitive function tests.

claims.claim: In the elevated plus maze test, Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice entered the open arms less frequently and traveled shorter distance in the open arms than WT mice.
claims.source: Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice entered the open arms and clear chamber less frequently and traveled shorter distance in the open arms and clear chamber than WT mice (Figure 4A–D; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–D).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by elevated plus maze test data shown in Figure 4A,B.

claims.claim: In the light-dark chamber test, Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice made less transitions between the light and dark chambers and traveled shorter distance in the light chamber than WT mice.
claims.source: Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice entered the open arms and clear chamber less frequently and traveled shorter distance in the open arms and clear chamber than WT mice (Figure 4A–D; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–D).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by light-dark chamber test data shown in Figure 4C,D.

claims.claim: The elevated plus maze and light-dark chamber tests confirm the heightened anxiety in Stxbp1 haploinsufficient mice.
claims.source: Hence, these results confirm the heightened anxiety in Stxbp1 haploinsufficient mice and are consistent with the previous studies (Hager et al., 2014; Miyamoto et al., 2017; Kovacevic et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the anxiety tests and is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: In the hole-board test, Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice made more repetitive nose pokes than WT mice across many holes.
claims.source: We analyzed the repetitive nose pokes (i.e.,≥2 consecutive pokes) into the same hole as a measure of repetitive behaviors. The mutant mice made more repetitive nose pokes than WT mice across many holes (Figure 4G), indicating that Stxbp1 haploinsufficiency in mice causes abnormal stereotypy and repetitive behaviors, a psychiatric feature observed in about 20% of the STXBP1 encephalopathy patients (Stamberger et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by hole-board test data shown in Figure 4G.

claims.claim: Stxbp1 haploinsufficiency in mice causes abnormal stereotypy and repetitive behaviors.
claims.source: We analyzed the repetitive nose pokes (i.e.,≥2 consecutive pokes) into the same hole as a measure of repetitive behaviors. The mutant mice made more repetitive nose pokes than WT mice across many holes (Figure 4G), indicating that Stxbp1 haploinsufficiency in mice causes abnormal stereotypy and repetitive behaviors, a psychiatric feature observed in about 20% of the STXBP1 encephalopathy patients (Stamberger et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the hole-board test data.

claims.claim: In the resident-intruder test, male resident Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice were more likely to attack and spent more time attacking the intruders as compared to WT mice.
claims.source: As compared to WT mice, male resident Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice were more likely to attack and spent more time attacking the intruders (Figure 5A–C).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by resident-intruder test data shown in Figure 5A–C.

claims.claim: In the tube test, when Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice were placed against their sex- and age-matched WT littermates, Stxbp1 haploinsufficient mice won more competitions despite their smaller body sizes.
claims.source: Another paradigm to assess aggression and social dominance is the tube test, in which two mice are released into the opposite ends of a tube, and the more dominant and aggressive mouse will win the competition by pushing its opponent out of the tube. When Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice were placed against their sex- and age-matched WT littermates, Stxbp1 haploinsufficient mice won more competitions despite their smaller body sizes (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by tube test data shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: Stxbp1 haploinsufficiency elevates innate aggression in mice.
claims.source: Thus, Stxbp1 haploinsufficiency elevates innate aggression in mice.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the aggression tests.

claims.claim: In the three-chamber test, like WT mice, Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice preferred to interact with the partner mice rather than the objects.
claims.source: Like WT mice, Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice preferred to interact with the partner mice rather than the objects (Figure 5E), indicating that Stxbp1 haploinsufficiency does not compromise general sociability.
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by three-chamber test data shown in Figure 5E.

claims.claim: Stxbp1 haploinsufficiency does not compromise general sociability.
claims.source: Like WT mice, Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice preferred to interact with the partner mice rather than the objects (Figure 5E), indicating that Stxbp1 haploinsufficiency does not compromise general sociability.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the three-chamber test data.

claims.claim: In the partition test, both WT and Stxbp1tm1d/+ mice preferentially interacted more with the novel partner mice.
claims.source: Furthermore, we used the partition test to examine the preference for social novelty, in which a mouse is allowed to interact with a familiar or novel partner mouse. Both WT and Stxbp1tm1d/+ mice preferentially interacted more with the novel partner mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by partition test data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: The general sociability and interest in social novelty are normal in Stxbp1 haploinsufficient mice.
claims.source: These results indicate that the general sociability and interest in social novelty are normal in Stxbp1 haploinsufficient mice.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the social interaction tests.

claims.claim: In the Nestlet shredding test, Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice consistently scored lower than WT mice at all time points.
claims.source: We provided a Nestlet (pressed cotton square) to each mouse in the home cage and scored the degree of shredding and nest quality after 24, 48, and 72 hr (Figure 5F). Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice consistently scored lower than WT mice at all time points (Figure 5G).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by Nestlet shredding test data shown in Figure 5G.

claims.claim: In the marble burying test, Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice buried fewer marbles than WT mice.
claims.source: In the marble burying test, the Stxbp1tm1d/+ and Stxbp1tm1a/+ mice buried fewer marbles than WT mice (Figure 5H).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by marble burying test data shown in Figure 5H.

claims.claim: Stxbp1tm1d/+ mice exhibited cortical hyperexcitability and several epileptiform activities.
claims.source: Stxbp1tm1d/+ mice exhibited cortical hyperexcitability and several epileptiform activities.
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results and is supported by EEG/EMG data in Figure 6.

claims.claim: Stxbp1tm1d/+ mice had numerous spike-wave discharges (SWDs) that typically were 3–6 Hz and lasted 1–2 s.
claims.source: First, they had numerous spike-wave discharges (SWDs) that typically were 3–6 Hz and lasted 1–2 s (Figure 6C,E,F).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by EEG data shown in Figure 6C,E,F.

claims.claim: The frequency of SWD episodes in Stxbp1tm1d/+ mice was more than 40-fold higher than that in WT mice.
claims.source: On average, the frequency of SWD episodes in Stxbp1tm1d/+ mice was more than 40-fold higher than that in WT mice (Figure 6E,F).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by EEG data shown in Figure 6E,F.

claims.claim: SWDs frequently occurred in a cluster manner in Stxbp1tm1d/+ mice, which never occurred in WT mice.
claims.source: Importantly, SWDs frequently occurred in a cluster manner (i.e.,≥5 episodes with an inter-episode-interval of ≤60 s) in Stxbp1tm1d/+ mice, which never occurred in WT mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 1; Video 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by EEG data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and Video 1.

claims.claim: 56 episodes of SWDs from 10 out of 13 Stxbp1tm1d/+ mice lasted more than 4 s, among which 54 episodes occurred during REM sleep.
claims.source: Furthermore, 56 episodes of SWDs from 10 out of 13 Stxbp1tm1d/+ mice lasted more than 4 s, among which 54 episodes occurred during rapid eye movement (REM) sleep (Figure 6D; Video 2) and the other two episodes occurred when mice were awake.
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by EEG data shown in Figure 6D and Video 2.

claims.claim: Stxbp1tm1d/+ mice experienced frequent myoclonic seizures that manifested as sudden jumps or more subtle, involuntary muscle jerks associated with EEG discharges.
claims.source: Second, Stxbp1tm1d/+ mice experienced frequent myoclonic seizures that manifested as sudden jumps or more subtle, involuntary muscle jerks associated with EEG discharges (Figure 6G,H).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by EEG/EMG data shown in Figure 6G,H.

claims.claim: Myoclonic jumps were observed in all 13 recorded Stxbp1tm1d/+ mice and the majority of episodes occurred during REM or NREM sleep.
claims.source: The large movement artifacts associated with the myoclonic jumps precluded proper interpretation of EEG signals, but this type of myoclonic seizures was observed in all 13 recorded Stxbp1tm1d/+ mice and the majority of episodes occurred during REM or non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep (Figure 6I; Video 3).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by EEG/EMG data shown in Figure 6I and Video 3.

claims.claim: The more subtle myoclonic jerks occurred frequently and often in clusters in Stxbp1tm1d/+ mice, whereas only isolated events were observed in WT mice at a much lower frequency.
claims.source: Moreover, the more subtle myoclonic jerks occurred frequently and often in clusters in Stxbp1tm1d/+ mice, whereas only isolated events were observed in WT mice at a much lower frequency (Figure 6H,J; Video 4).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by EEG/EMG data shown in Figure 6H,J and Video 4.

claims.claim: EEG and EMG recordings showed that the cortical EEG spikes associated with the myoclonic jerks occurred before or simultaneously with the neck muscle EMG discharges.
claims.source: EEG and EMG recordings showed that the cortical EEG spikes associated with the myoclonic jerks occurred before or simultaneously with the neck muscle EMG discharges (Figure 6H), consistent with the cortical or subcortical origins of myoclonuses, respectively (Avanzini et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by EEG/EMG data shown in Figure 6H.

claims.claim: Immunostaining of a pan-neuronal marker NeuN revealed a grossly normal cytoarchitecture and cortical lamination in adult Stxbp1tm1d/+ mice.
claims.source: Immunostaining of a pan-neuronal marker NeuN revealed a grossly normal cytoarchitecture and cortical lamination in adult Stxbp1tm1d/+ mice (Figure 7A,B).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 7A,B.

claims.claim: The densities of cortical neurons and two major classes of inhibitory neurons, Pv and Sst interneurons, were similar between Stxbp1tm1d/+ and WT mice.
claims.source: The densities of cortical neurons and two major classes of inhibitory neurons, Pv and Sst interneurons, were similar between Stxbp1tm1d/+ and WT mice (Figure 7B–D).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 7B–D.

claims.claim: Stxbp1 haploinsufficiency does not appear to affect cortical neuron survival and migration.
claims.source: Thus, Stxbp1 haploinsufficiency does not appear to affect cortical neuron survival and migration.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the immunostaining data showing normal neuron densities.

claims.claim: The connectivity rate of Pv interneurons to pyramidal neurons was unaltered in Stxbp1tm1d/+ mice.
claims.source: The connectivity rate of Pv interneurons to pyramidal neurons was unaltered in Stxbp1tm1d/+;Rosa26tdTomato/+;PvCre/+ mice (Figure 8B), but the unitary connection strength was reduced by 45% as compared to Stxbp1+/+;Rosa26tdTomato/+;PvCre/+ mice (Figure 8C).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 8B.

claims.claim: The unitary connection strength from Pv interneurons to pyramidal neurons was reduced by 45% in Stxbp1tm1d/+ mice as compared to WT mice.
claims.source: The connectivity rate of Pv interneurons to pyramidal neurons was unaltered in Stxbp1tm1d/+;Rosa26tdTomato/+;PvCre/+ mice (Figure 8B), but the unitary connection strength was reduced by 45% as compared to Stxbp1+/+;Rosa26tdTomato/+;PvCre/+ mice (Figure 8C).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 8C.

claims.claim: Stxbp1tm1d/+ mice showed a 26% reduction in the connectivity rate of Sst interneurons to pyramidal neurons.
claims.source: In contrast, Stxbp1tm1d/+;Rosa26tdTomato/+;SstCre/+ mice showed a 26% reduction in the connectivity rate of Sst interneurons to pyramidal neurons (Figure 8F), but the unitary connection strength was normal (Figure 8G).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 8F.

claims.claim: The unitary connection strength from Sst interneurons to pyramidal neurons was normal in Stxbp1tm1d/+ mice.
claims.source: In contrast, Stxbp1tm1d/+;Rosa26tdTomato/+;SstCre/+ mice showed a 26% reduction in the connectivity rate of Sst interneurons to pyramidal neurons (Figure 8F), but the unitary connection strength was normal (Figure 8G).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 8G.

claims.claim: The short-term synaptic depression of both Pv and Sst inhibitory connections during the train of stimulations was normal in Stxbp1tm1d/+ mice.
claims.source: The short-term synaptic depression of both inhibitory connections during the train of stimulations was normal (Figure 8D,H).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 8D,H.

claims.claim: The spontaneous excitatory postsynaptic currents (sEPSCs) in Pv and Sst interneurons did not show any significant changes of either amplitude or frequency in Stxbp1tm1d/+ mice.
claims.source: Furthermore, we recorded the spontaneous excitatory postsynaptic currents (sEPSCs) in Pv and Sst interneurons and did not observe any significant changes of either amplitude or frequency in the mutant mice (Figure 8—figure supplement 2), suggesting that the excitatory drive onto interneurons is normal in Stxbp1 haploinsufficient mice.
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The excitatory drive onto interneurons is normal in Stxbp1 haploinsufficient mice.
claims.source: Furthermore, we recorded the spontaneous excitatory postsynaptic currents (sEPSCs) in Pv and Sst interneurons and did not observe any significant changes of either amplitude or frequency in the mutant mice (Figure 8—figure supplement 2), suggesting that the excitatory drive onto interneurons is normal in Stxbp1 haploinsufficient mice.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the sEPSC data.

claims.claim: The average amplitude, charge, and decay time constant of Pv interneurons-mediated quantal IPSCs were all similar between Stxbp1tm1d/+ and WT mice.
claims.source: We mathematically subtracted the mIPSCs recorded during the baseline period (i.e., before blue light stimulation) from those recorded during blue light stimulation to obtain the average amplitude, charge, and decay time constant of Pv interneurons-mediated quantal IPSCs (Figure 9B), which were all similar between Stxbp1tm1d/+;PvCre/+ and Stxbp1+/+;PvCre/+ mice (Figure 9E).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the results and supported by optogenetic electrophysiology data shown in Figure 9E.

claims.claim: The average amplitude, charge, and decay time constant of quantal IPSCs mediated by Sst interneurons were normal in Stxbp1tm1d/+ mice.
claims.source: Using this optogenetic method, we also found that the average amplitude, charge, and decay time constant of quantal IPSCs mediated by Sst interneurons were normal in Stxbp1tm1d/+;SstCre/+ mice (Figure 9C,D,F).

results.result: Two new Stxbp1 haploinsufficiency mouse models (tm1d and tm1a) were generated and validated. Homozygous mutants died at birth, while heterozygous mice showed 40-50% reduction in Stxbp1 protein levels in most brain regions at 3 months of age.
results.evaluation: Claims C21-C25 are well-supported by Western blot data (Figure 1 and supplements) showing protein absence in homozygotes and ~50% reduction in heterozygotes at embryonic day 17.5, and 40-50% reduction in adult brain regions. The genetic characterization is rigorous with appropriate controls and multiple antibodies.

results.result: Stxbp1 haploinsufficient mice exhibit reduced survival (40-43% of expected at weaning) and consistently lower body weights (~20% less than WT littermates).
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C28 are supported by genotyping data (Figure 1D, supplement 2A) showing deviation from Mendelian ratios and body weight measurements (Figure 1F) across ages. The postnatal lethality is incompletely penetrant as some mutants survive to adulthood (Figure 1—supplement 2B).

results.result: Stxbp1 haploinsufficient mice develop progressive hindlimb clasping starting at 4 weeks of age, with nearly complete penetrance by 3 months.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C30 are supported by longitudinal observations documented in Figure 1E,G showing age-dependent progression of hindlimb clasping. This phenotype is consistent with dystonia/spasticity observed in human patients.

results.result: Stxbp1 haploinsufficient mice exhibit motor dysfunction characterized by hyperactivity, increased anxiety, reduced grip strength, impaired fine motor coordination (foot slips), and reduced agility (vertical pole test), but no ataxia.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C36 are supported by comprehensive behavioral testing data (Figure 2, supplements) including open-field, grip strength, foot slip, and vertical pole tests. The rotarod test (Figure 2—supplement 1) appropriately shows no ataxia. Sample sizes are adequate (n=19-41 per group) and both mouse lines show consistent phenotypes.

results.result: Sensory functions (acoustic startle, nociception) and sensorimotor gating (pre-pulse inhibition) are normal in Stxbp1 haploinsufficient mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C40 are supported by acoustic startle, pre-pulse inhibition, and hot plate test data (Figure 2—supplement 2). These negative results are important controls demonstrating that cognitive and motor deficits are not due to sensory impairments.

results.result: Stxbp1 haploinsufficient mice show severe impairments in both long-term and short-term recognition memory (novel object recognition) and associative memory (contextual and cued fear conditioning), but intact working memory (Y-maze).
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C45 are supported by novel object recognition (Figure 3A, supplement 1A,D) and fear conditioning data (Figure 3B-E, supplement 1E) at multiple time points and ages. The Y-maze data (Figure 3—supplement 1F) appropriately shows preserved working memory. Sample sizes are adequate (n=12-30 per group).

results.result: Stxbp1 haploinsufficient mice exhibit heightened anxiety-like behaviors in elevated plus maze and light-dark chamber tests.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C48 are supported by elevated plus maze (Figure 4A,B) and light-dark chamber (Figure 4C,D) data showing reduced exploration of aversive areas. This confirms the anxiety phenotype initially observed in the open-field test and is consistent with previous studies (C48 cites supporting literature).

results.result: Stxbp1 haploinsufficient mice display increased repetitive behaviors as measured by repetitive nose pokes in the hole-board test.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C50 are supported by hole-board test data (Figure 4G) showing increased repetitive nose pokes across multiple holes. The analysis appropriately defines repetitive behavior as ≥2 consecutive pokes into the same hole. This phenotype parallels stereotypies observed in ~20% of human patients.

results.result: Stxbp1 haploinsufficient mice exhibit elevated innate aggression in resident-intruder and tube tests.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C53 are supported by resident-intruder test data (Figure 5A-C) showing increased attack frequency and duration, and tube test data (Figure 5D) showing increased winning despite smaller body size. The tube test result is particularly compelling as it controls for body size differences.

results.result: General sociability and preference for social novelty are normal in Stxbp1 haploinsufficient mice as measured by three-chamber and partition tests.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C57 are supported by three-chamber test (Figure 5E) and partition test (Figure 5—supplement 1A) data. Mutant mice show normal or even enhanced social interaction, though the authors appropriately note that increased aggression may confound interpretation of enhanced interaction time.

results.result: Stxbp1 haploinsufficient mice show reduced nest building (Nestlet shredding) and marble burying behaviors.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C59 are supported by Nestlet shredding (Figure 5F,G) and marble burying (Figure 5H) data. The authors appropriately note that motor deficits may contribute to these phenotypes, making interpretation as purely psychiatric measures uncertain.

results.result: Stxbp1tm1d/+ mice exhibit cortical hyperexcitability with numerous spike-wave discharges (SWDs) occurring at >40-fold higher frequency than WT, often in clusters, with some long-duration episodes (>4s) occurring predominantly during REM sleep.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C64 are supported by comprehensive EEG/EMG data (Figure 6A-F, supplement 1, Videos 1-2) from 13 mutant and 11 WT mice recorded for ≥72 hours. The clustering analysis (Figure 6—supplement 1) uses appropriate statistical simulations (10^6 iterations) to demonstrate non-random clustering. The characterization of SWD frequency, duration, and behavioral state is rigorous.

results.result: Stxbp1tm1d/+ mice experience frequent myoclonic seizures (sudden jumps and subtle jerks) with EEG discharges preceding or simultaneous with EMG activity, occurring predominantly during REM/NREM sleep.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C68 are supported by EEG/EMG data (Figure 6G-J, Videos 3-4) showing myoclonic seizures in all 13 recorded mutant mice. The temporal relationship between EEG spikes and EMG discharges (Figure 6H) is consistent with cortical/subcortical origins. The clustering of subtle jerks and their predominance during sleep are well-documented.

results.result: Cortical cytoarchitecture, lamination, and densities of total neurons, Pv interneurons, and Sst interneurons are normal in Stxbp1tm1d/+ mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C71 are supported by immunohistochemistry data (Figure 7) showing no differences in NeuN, Pv, or Sst cell densities between mutant and WT mice. The quantification methods are appropriate (manual counting for interneurons, automated surface detection for total neurons with <10% error rate). This is an important negative result ruling out gross developmental defects.

results.result: Pv interneuron to pyramidal neuron connectivity is normal in Stxbp1tm1d/+ mice, but unitary connection strength is reduced by 45%, with normal short-term depression.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C73, C76 are supported by paired recording data (Figure 8A-D) showing normal connectivity rate (27/33 vs 26/32 connections) but significantly reduced uIPSC amplitude (median 217.3 vs 127.1 pA, p<0.01). The short-term plasticity analysis is appropriate. Sample sizes are adequate for paired recordings.

results.result: Sst interneuron to pyramidal neuron connectivity is reduced by 26% in Stxbp1tm1d/+ mice, but unitary connection strength is normal, with normal short-term depression.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C75, C76 are supported by paired recording data (Figure 8E-H) showing reduced connectivity rate (25/36 vs 34/36 connections, p<0.05) but normal uIPSC amplitude (median 83.5 vs 68.0 pA, p>0.05). This represents a distinct mechanism from Pv synapses. The finding is unexpected and novel.

results.result: Spontaneous excitatory drive onto Pv and Sst interneurons (sEPSC frequency and amplitude) is normal in Stxbp1tm1d/+ mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C78 are supported by sEPSC recordings (Figure 8—supplement 2) showing no differences in frequency or amplitude in either interneuron type. This is an important control demonstrating that the inhibitory deficits are not secondary to altered excitatory input onto interneurons.

results.result: Quantal IPSC properties (amplitude, charge, decay time) from both Pv and Sst interneurons are normal in Stxbp1tm1d/+ mice, indicating intact postsynaptic inhibitory transmission.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C81 are supported by optogenetic isolation of quantal IPSCs (Figure 9) using a novel method combining ChR2 stimulation with TTX and Sr2+ substitution. The method appropriately isolates asynchronous release from specific interneuron types. Normal quantal properties indicate presynaptic deficits rather than postsynaptic changes.

results.result: The reduction in Pv synapse strength likely reflects decreased readily releasable vesicles or release probability, while reduced Sst connectivity suggests fewer inhibitory inputs onto pyramidal neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C83 are logical inferences supported by the combined data: normal Pv connectivity + reduced strength + normal quantal size = presynaptic release deficit (C82); normal Sst cell density + reduced connectivity + normal strength = fewer synapses (C83). These interpretations are reasonable given the data.

results.result: Impaired cortical inhibition from both Pv and Sst interneurons likely constitutes a key cellular mechanism underlying cortical hyperexcitability, seizures, and neurobehavioral deficits in Stxbp1 haploinsufficient mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C84, C86, C91 represent the central mechanistic conclusion linking reduced GABAergic inhibition to disease phenotypes. This is well-supported by the convergence of electrophysiology data (reduced inhibition from both interneuron types) and phenotypic data (seizures, hyperexcitability, behavioral deficits). The logic is sound though causality is not directly demonstrated.

results.result: Stxbp1 haploinsufficient mice are construct- and face-valid models of STXBP1 encephalopathy, recapitulating cardinal features including cognitive deficits, motor dysfunction, psychiatric symptoms, and seizures.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C85 are supported by the comprehensive phenotypic characterization across multiple domains (Figures 1-6) showing that mutant mice exhibit all key features of human STXBP1 encephalopathy. The construct validity (haploinsufficiency mechanism) and face validity (phenotypic similarity) are well-established. The parallel characterization of two independent lines enhances robustness.

results.result: The differential effects on Pv (reduced strength) versus Sst (reduced connectivity) interneuron-mediated inhibition suggest synapse-specific functions of Stxbp1.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C88 are supported by the distinct mechanisms of inhibitory dysfunction at Pv versus Sst synapses (Figures 8-9). This is a novel finding suggesting cell-type or synapse-type specific roles for Stxbp1 beyond its canonical function in vesicle release. The interpretation is reasonable though speculative.

results.result: The unexpected reduction in Sst interneuron connectivity suggests Stxbp1 may regulate processes beyond presynaptic transmitter release, potentially including synapse formation or maintenance.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C90 are speculative interpretations of the reduced Sst connectivity. While the finding is unexpected and novel, the authors acknowledge this is speculation. Additional morphological and structural analyses would be needed to confirm involvement in synapse formation/maintenance. The claim that Stxbp1 has not been implicated in synapse formation (C89) may overlook relevant literature.

results.result: Background claims establishing STXBP1's role in neurotransmitter release, the clinical features of STXBP1 encephalopathy in humans, and limitations of previous mouse models.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C8-C20 are background/context claims supported by appropriate citations to prior literature. These establish the rationale for the study. The citations appear appropriate and the claims about human disease features and previous mouse models are well-documented in the literature.
